findings.title: Adding an abstract SPI method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: `CryptoProvider` is a public ServiceLoader SPI, and adding `order()` as an abstract method makes every provider compiled against the previous interface incompatible. During `CryptoIntegration.init`, the comparator invokes `order()` on such a provider and throws `AbstractMethodError`, preventing startup even when that provider was the only valid provider before this change. Make this a default method with a legacy-safe priority (or otherwise provide a compatibility adapter) so existing implementations remain loadable.

findings.title: Equal-priority crypto providers are silently selected by classpath order
findings.body: The new selection logic accepts multiple providers with the same highest priority and chooses whichever ServiceLoader returns first. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider`, and `FIPS1402Provider` are all assigned priority 200, so a classpath containing both default and FIPS providers no longer fails fast as it did previously; it can select the non-FIPS default provider based on classpath/resource ordering. This can silently disable the intended FIPS crypto integration. Reject ties for the highest priority (while still allowing lower-priority providers such as the authz client provider), or make selection explicitly configured and deterministic.

findings.title: ECDSA raw signature conversion accepts and ignores trailing signature bytes
findings.body: `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` copies exactly `signLength` bytes but never verifies that `signature.length` equals `signLength`. Any bytes after the expected R||S value are silently discarded, so distinct raw JOSE ECDSA signature values with the same prefix are converted to the same DER value and can be accepted by a verifier. Short inputs also fail with an unchecked array-copy exception rather than being treated as invalid signatures. Validate the exact fixed signature length up front and throw the declared `IOException` for malformed input.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns an unrelated JDK keystore provider
findings.body: The `CryptoProvider` contract states that this method returns the Bouncy Castle provider, but this implementation returns the provider backing the JVM's default keystore. On a normal JVM that is typically `SUN`, not Bouncy Castle. Once this provider is selected by `CryptoIntegration`, callers relying on this method to obtain Bouncy Castle functionality receive an unrelated provider and may use unsupported algorithms or fail unexpectedly. A provider with no Bouncy Castle integration should report that absence consistently (as the Elytron provider does) or supply an actual Bouncy Castle provider.

findings.title: ES384 and ES512 tests generate a default EC key instead of the algorithm's curve
findings.body: All three tests use an unparameterized `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")`; in common JDKs this produces a P-256 key. Consequently the ES384 and ES512 cases sign P-256-sized R/S values and merely zero-pad them to 48 and 66 bytes, rather than exercising P-384 and P-521 signatures. In particular, the ES512 test does not cover the long-form DER sequence length used by real P-521 signatures, and it only round-trips through the same custom encoder/decoder rather than verifying the generated DER with the public key. Generate `secp256r1`, `secp384r1`, and `secp521r1` keys respectively and verify the converted DER signatures end-to-end.
